adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that changing BROKER_PUBLIC on a realm-level (unlinked) provider won't invalidate the cache. However, examining the diff shows that getLoginPredicate() now includes `.and(idp -> idp.getOrganizationId() == null || Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC)))`. For a realm-level provider (organizationId == null), this predicate always returns true regardless of BROKER_PUBLIC value, because the first condition `idp.getOrganizationId() == null` is true. The cache invalidation logic correctly handles this case because realm-level providers always satisfy the login predicate.

adjudication.rationale: The finding misunderstands the code logic. The `getLoginPredicate()` tests whether an IDP qualifies for login based on its properties (enabled, hideOnLogin, linkOnly, etc.). The invalidation logic at line 405 correctly skips invalidation only when BOTH original and updated don't qualify for login - meaning neither was nor will be in the login cache. If an IDP transitions from qualifying to not-qualifying (or vice versa), one of the predicates will be true and the other false, so the early return won't trigger and invalidation will occur. The 'wrapped isEnabled' concern is also misplaced - the predicate is applied to the model objects passed to the method, not to cached/wrapped versions. The test cases in the diff demonstrate this works correctly for various transitions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: model/infinispan/src/main/java/org/keycloak/models/cache/infinispan/idp/InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.java:239 — P2 confidence 75 mode advisory: Concurrent population resurrects invalidated login results because `query = new IdentityProviderListQuery(loaded, cacheKey, getRealm(), searchKey, cached, query);` copies the earlier query into an entry published by `cache.addRevisioned(query, cache.getCurrentCounter());`; trigger: request A reads a query containing organization X, request B creates a login IDP for X and commits its invalidation, then A fills an uncached organization Y after `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` and obtains the new revision; consequence: X's old ID set is republished under that fresh revision and subsequent successful login-page requests omit the newly created provider until another invalidation or eviction, while the null-ID fallback cannot detect an omitted provider; strongest counterargument: revision-aware insertion rejects obsolete cache entries, rebuttal: this branch obtains `loaded` after the invalidation and passes the current counter, so the old results copied from `query` carry the new revision instead of their original revision.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real race condition in the cache population logic. Looking at lines 230-237 in the diff, when a cache entry exists but the current search key is not cached, the code: 1) invalidates the cache key, 2) gets a new revision, 3) fetches fresh data for the new search key, 4) creates a new IdentityProviderListQuery passing the old `query` as the last parameter (which copies its existing search results). The constructor `new IdentityProviderListQuery(loaded, cacheKey, getRealm(), searchKey, cached, query)` copies the old query's cached results for other search keys. If between step 1 and step 4, another thread invalidates the cache due to an IDP change, the old stale results from the original query get republished with the new revision obtained after invalidation. The `cache.addRevisioned(query, cache.getCurrentCounter())` uses the current counter which is after the invalidation, so the stale data gets a fresh revision and won't be rejected. This is a legitimate concurrency bug where invalidated data can be resurrected.

adjudication_records.issue_text: model/infinispan/src/main/java/org/keycloak/models/cache/infinispan/idp/InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.java:405 — P2, confidence 75: `if (!getLoginPredicate().test(original) && !getLoginPredicate().test(updated)) {` preserves a cached public login entry when an administrator sets BROKER_PUBLIC=false on an otherwise enabled IdP while its organization is disabled, because original comes from getById with organization-aware isEnabled=false and updated fails the public predicate, so re-enabling the organization exposes the now-private provider on the unauthenticated login page until that query is invalidated or evicted; the strongest counterargument is that getById refreshes the model and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean rechecks isEnabled, but that check becomes true after re-enablement and neither the cache-hit loop nor the ALL/ORG_ONLY login filters recheck BROKER_PUBLIC, so the fresh private model is still rendered.

adjudication.rationale: The finding misunderstands the code flow. When BROKER_PUBLIC is set to false on an IDP, the getLoginPredicate() includes a check for 'idp.getOrganizationId() == null || Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))'. If BROKER_PUBLIC becomes false for an org-linked IDP, getLoginPredicate().test(updated) will return false (since organizationId is not null and BROKER_PUBLIC is false). This means the condition '!getLoginPredicate().test(original) && !getLoginPredicate().test(updated)' won't be satisfied if original was a login IDP, so the cache WILL be invalidated. The scenario described requires original to fail the predicate (due to org being disabled making isEnabled=false), but the predicate checks the model's properties directly, not the wrapped isEnabled state. The finding constructs an overly complex scenario that doesn't match how the code actually works.
